sections.h2: Which Summit County office do I call about real estate taxes?
sections.html:
Start with the Summit County Fiscal Office, which houses Auditor, Treasurer and Recorder divisions under a single elected Fiscal Officer. The Auditor division sets values and rates, the Treasurer division issues bills and takes money, and a Board of Revision hears value disputes.

The one-office setup comes from the county charter. Wikipedia notes that Summit and Cuyahoga are Ohio's only charter counties, and that Summit's fiscal officer does the work other counties spread across a separate auditor, treasurer and recorder. An executive and an eleven-member council stand in for the usual three commissioners.

Renovation of the Ohio Building at 175 S. Main St. in Akron pushed the Fiscal Office's divisions into temporary quarters, so phone first. The contact page carries these lines:

  • Main office: 1-888-388-5613
  • Treasurer: 330-643-2588
  • Real Estate and Appraisal, which handles homestead and assessments: 330-643-2710
  • Board of Revision: 330-926-2559 or bor@summitoh.net
  • Delinquent Tax Department: 330-643-2600

sections.h2: What kind of county is Summit for a house sale?
sections.html:
QuickFacts estimates about 538,000 residents in 2025 on 412.79 square miles of land, 0.4 percent under the 2020 base. Owner-occupied homes make up 67.5 percent of the stock, the median value of those homes is $208,700, and renters pay a median $1,026. Median household income is $71,622. Those medians cover the whole county, so any one street may differ.

Akron is the seat and largest city. The county dates to March 3, 1840, cut from Medina, Portage and Stark, and takes its name from the high point of the Ohio and Erie Canal. Cuyahoga Valley National Park fills much of the north. Barberton, Cuyahoga Falls, Fairlawn, Green, Hudson, Macedonia, Munroe Falls, New Franklin, Norton, Stow, Tallmadge and Twinsburg are the other cities, linked by I-76, I-77, I-271, I-480 and the Ohio Turnpike.

Seventy-four taxing authorities share the bill, per the Fiscal Office: the county, 5 county agencies, 26 school districts, 8 library districts, 14 cities, 8 villages, 9 townships, a water district, a fire district and a recreation district. The two leading digits of a parcel number identify your taxing district, and that district decides the rate.

sections.h2: What goes into a Summit County tax bill?
sections.html:
Ohio taxes 35 percent of appraised value. The rate stacks up levies that local voters approved. The Fiscal Officer states on the tax rates page that the office has no power to raise or lower taxes, and the page links three years of effective rate summaries. It sorts levies into five kinds:

  • Additional: new money for a taxing body, so bills rise.
  • Renewal: the same yield as an expiring levy.
  • Replacement: swaps in current values for a levy built on old ones, so bills move with the market.
  • Emergency: schools only, a fixed yearly sum over a stated span.
  • Bond: covers principal and interest on a permanent improvement.

The bill explanation lists the summary of charges: reduction factor, non-business credit, owner-occupancy credit, homestead reduction, current net taxes and current assessments. A bill covers the year before, because Ohio collects one year in arrears. Akron residents with an assessment question call 330-375-2484, and everyone else calls 330-643-2645.

sections.h2: How late can I pay, and what does a miss cost?
sections.html:
Dates print on the bill. The Fiscal Office FAQ says there is no grace period and that never receiving a bill is no defense. A missed first half draws a 10 percent penalty. Miss the second half too and the full unpaid current balance, first-half amount included, takes another 10 percent. Per R.C. 323.121(C), paying everything within ten days after a deadline halves that penalty.

Payment channels named in the FAQ:

  • A counter visit to the Treasurer division, checks payable to the Fiscal Officer or Fiscal Office.
  • Mail with a U.S. postmark on or before the deadline. Private meter stamps are rejected.
  • A bank listed on your bill, available only while a collection is open.
  • Phone or web through Official Payments Corporation, which charges 1 percent on debit (minimum $3.95), 2.75 percent on credit (minimum $3.95) or $1.00 per electronic check, per the online payments page.
  • Cash at a MoneyGram location, plus a service fee.

Summit's charter lets it run a prepayment plan, the Real Estate Discount program. Owners with no delinquency sign up between July 1 and October 31 for a first half, or between January 1 and March 31 for a second half, pay on five of six coupons and earn credit on the early money. Missing the last coupon forfeits the credit.

sections.h2: What is the route for disputing a Summit County valuation?
sections.html:
Use the Board of Revision, whose window runs from the first of January through the end of March. It rules on value alone and never on the tax amount, and the owner has to prove the claim with paperwork.

Summit County Board of Revision at a glance, per the Fiscal Office complaint page
ItemDetail
WindowJanuary 1 to March 31
DeliveryMail postmarked by the deadline, a counter visit, or Smartfile online
SeatsFiscal Officer, County Executive, Clerk of Courts, or designees
ProofHanded in, mailed, or uploaded with an online filing
Legal weightFiling starts a legal proceeding

Values are redone every six years, with an update in year three, by comparing a parcel with neighborhood sales. Permits tip off the office to new building. Rewiring, replumbing, framing or foundation work can raise value, while a new roof or routine remodeling does not.

With a complaint pending, R.C. 5715.19 allows you to tender tax computed on your claimed value, with interest on any shortfall if the final number lands higher. Evidence withheld from the board can be excluded on appeal. For storm, fire, flood or demolition damage, file DTE Form 26 by December 31 (damage in the year's first nine months) or by January 31 (last three months).

sections.h2: Which tax reductions can a Summit County seller or heir use?
sections.html:
The homestead exemption removes the first $29,000 of appraised value on a single-family home from tax, and the office puts average savings at $535 yearly. It covers owners 65 by December 31, the permanently and totally disabled, veterans rated 100 percent for service-connected disability, and spouses of first responders who died on duty. Veterans see $58,000 exempted. The 2026 income ceiling for age and disability claims is $41,000, using the owner's and spouse's Ohio adjusted gross income.

The owner-occupancy reduction needs you to own and live in the home on January 1, with the application in by December 31. Rentals are out. It ends when the property transfers, so an incoming owner-occupant files again.

At transfer, R.C. 319.202 has the buyer's conveyance statement confirm that the seller was asked about these reductions. If the house gets one, a sworn note estimating the amount travels with it. Your title company will request the answer.

sections.h2: What can I do about back taxes on a Summit County house?
sections.html:
The Delinquent Tax Payment Plan, started in 1987, takes owners who missed a half and sets monthly installments. The old balance freezes in a special account with no added interest, leftover interest is abated at completion, and new bills must be paid on time.

The office sells tax certificate liens each late October. Paying in full or entering a plan keeps a lien off that sale. If you would rather sell, ask the title company to request a payoff figure from the Treasurer division and settle it at closing.

faqs.q: What is the late fee on Summit County property tax?
faqs.a: It is 10 percent of the unpaid half. Full payment within ten days after the deadline gets half of that penalty waived under state law.

faqs.q: Can I use the Real Estate Discount program while I owe back taxes?
faqs.a: No. Taxes must be current to enroll. Owners who are behind should ask about the Delinquent Tax Payment Plan.

faqs.q: How soon must I report fire or storm damage to the Fiscal Office?
faqs.a: File DTE Form 26 by December 31 for damage from January through September, or by January 31 of the following year for October through December damage. Send it to appraisedvalue@summitoh.net or mail it in.
The Fiscal Office property search finds it from a name, address or the number itself. Its first two digits name the taxing district.

faqs.q: Does a postmark on the due date count?
faqs.a: A Postal Service postmark on the due date counts, while a private meter mark does not. Under state law the earliest postmark on the envelope sets the payment date.
